## Introduction

Emily Dickinson is known for short poems about big subjects and for her heavy use of
the dash (`--`). In this project I use string functions and regular expressions to ask:

1. Which words does she use most?
2. How does her use of dashes compare across the three groups of poem files in the data?

## Data source

* **R package:** `DickinsonPoems` by Nicholas Horton, available at
  <https://github.com/Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems> and installed with
  `devtools::install_github("Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems")`.
* **Original source:** the Project Gutenberg edition of Emily Dickinson's poems,
  <https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12242/12242-h/12242-h.htm>.
* Each poem is stored as its own text file (like `gutenberg1.txt001`). I call the
  digit after "gutenberg" the "file group" (1, 2, or 3).

## Read in the data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(DickinsonPoems)

poems_raw <- tibble(file = list_poems()) |>
  mutate(raw = map_chr(file, \(f) str_flatten(get_poem(f), collapse = "\n")))
```

## Clean the data

Each poem starts with a Roman numeral like `XIX.`, then usually an ALL-CAPS title, then
the poem itself. I use regular expressions to pull these pieces apart.

* `(?<=gutenberg)\\d` is a **lookbehind**: it grabs the digit that comes right after
  the word "gutenberg" in the file name.
* `[IVXLC]+(?=\\.)` is a **lookahead**: it grabs the Roman numeral only if a period
  follows it.
* `[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]*` matches a line with no lowercase letters (the title).

```{r}
poems <- poems_raw |>
  mutate(
    raw = str_trim(raw),
    group = str_extract(file, "(?<=gutenberg)\\d"),
    group = str_c("File group ", group),
    roman = str_extract(raw, "^[IVXLC]+(?=\\.)"),
    body = str_trim(str_remove(raw, "^[IVXLC]+\\.")),
    title = str_extract(body, "^[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]*(?=\\n)"),
    text = str_trim(str_remove(body, "^[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]*\\n")),
    n_dashes = str_count(text, "--")
  ) |>
  select(file, group, roman, title, text, n_dashes)

head(poems)
```


## Question 1: Which words does she use most?

I pull out every word with the regular expression `[a-z']+` (letters and apostrophes),
then remove a short list of very common words so that the interesting words stand out.

```{r}
stop_words_small <- c("the", "and", "that", "with", "for", "was", "are", "but",
                      "not", "you", "all", "his", "her", "they", "this", "have",
                      "from", "will", "has", "had", "its", "were", "who", "when",
                      "then", "than", "there", "their", "she", "him", "our", "can",
                      "one", "would", "could", "what", "which", "upon", "thy",
                      "thee", "thou", "been", "into", "more", "does", "just")

all_words <- tibble(
  word = unlist(str_extract_all(str_to_lower(poems$text), "[a-z']+"))
)

top_words <- all_words |>
  filter(str_length(word) > 2, !word %in% stop_words_small) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12)

top_words
```

```{r}
top_words |>
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = word)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Dickinson's 12 Most Frequent Words",
    subtitle = "Very common words removed",
    x = "Number of times used",
    y = "Word"
  )
```


## Question 2: How does her use of dashes compare across file groups?

```{r}
dash_by_group <- poems |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    poems = n(),
    avg_dashes = mean(n_dashes)
  ) |>
  mutate(group = fct_reorder(group, avg_dashes))

dash_by_group
```

```{r}
ggplot(dash_by_group, aes(x = group, y = avg_dashes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Number of Dashes per Poem",
    subtitle = "Compared across the three file groups",
    x = "File group",
    y = "Average dashes per poem"
  )
```

## Bonus table: words right before a dash

A **lookahead** lets me grab the word before a `--` without including the dash itself.

```{r}
pre_dash <- tibble(
  word = unlist(str_extract_all(str_to_lower(poems$text), "[a-z']+(?=\\s*--)"))
) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)

pre_dash
```


## Conclusion

Dickinson returns to a small set of words again and again, and the dash is a regular
part of her style. A limitation is that my stop-word list is short and was written by
hand, so a few very common words may still appear in the results.
